claim: t-CyCIF generates up to 60-plex images using an iterative process in which conventional low-plex fluorescence images are repeatedly collected from the same sample and then assembled into a high-dimensional representation.
source: t-CyCIF generates up to 60-plex images using an iterative process (a cycle) in which conventional low-plex fluorescence images are repeatedly collected from the same sample and then assembled into a high-dimensional representation.
evidence: The abstract directly states the capability of t-CyCIF to generate 60-plex images through an iterative process.

claim: t-CyCIF requires no specialized instruments or reagents.
source: t-CyCIF requires no specialized instruments or reagents and is compatible with super-resolution imaging
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that t-CyCIF does not require specialized instruments or reagents.

claim: t-CyCIF is compatible with super-resolution imaging.
source: t-CyCIF requires no specialized instruments or reagents and is compatible with super-resolution imaging
evidence: The abstract explicitly states compatibility with super-resolution imaging.

claim: IHC is primarily a single-channel method where imaging multiple antigens usually involves the analysis of sequential tissue slices or harsh stripping protocols.
source: The potential of IHC to aid in diagnosis and prioritization of therapy is well established (Bodenmiller, 2016), but IHC is primarily a single-channel method: imaging multiple antigens usually involves the analysis of sequential tissue slices or harsh stripping protocols (although limited multiplexing is possible using IHC and bright-field imaging [Stack et al., 2014; Tsujikawa et al., 2017]).
evidence: The introduction describes the limitations of IHC as a single-channel method, citing published literature.

claim: Antibody detection via formation of a brown diamino-benzidine (DAB) or similar precipitates are less quantitative than fluorescence.
source: Antibody detection via formation of a brown diamino-benzidine (DAB) or similar precipitates are also less quantitative than fluorescence (Rimm, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites published work comparing DAB-based detection to fluorescence.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio often increases with cycle number in t-CyCIF due to progressive reductions in background intensity over the course of multiple rounds of fluorophore bleaching.
source: In t-CyCIF, the signal-to-noise ratio often increases with cycle number due to progressive reductions in background intensity over the course of multiple rounds of fluorophore bleaching.
evidence: The manuscript describes an observed phenomenon in t-CyCIF experiments.

claim: Auto-fluorescent features gradually disappear with increasing t-CyCIF cycle number.
source: This effect is visible in Figure 1B as the gradual disappearance of an auto-fluorescent feature (denoted by a dotted white oval and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1; see detailed analysis below).
evidence: The manuscript references Figure 1B showing the disappearance of auto-fluorescence.

claim: Background signal is reduced 10- to 100-fold with increasing number of bleaching cycles.
source: With increasing number of bleaching cycles, the background signal is reduced 10- to 100-fold.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1 caption states the quantitative reduction in background signal.

claim: The Zenon antibody labeling method is effective with 30–40% of the primary antibodies tested.
source: This method is effective with 30–40% of the primary antibodies that we have tested and potentially represents a simple way to label a wide range of primary antibodies with different fluorophores.
evidence: The manuscript reports the success rate of the Zenon method based on their testing.

claim: t-CyCIF can be performed on a variety of fluorescent microscopes including slide scanners, confocal microscopes, and structured illumination microscopes.
source: Imaging of t-CyCIF samples can be performed on a variety of fluorescent microscopes each of which represent a different tradeoff between data acquisition time, image resolution and sensitivity (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the compatibility of t-CyCIF with various microscope types.

claim: The efficiency of fluorophore inactivation by hydrogen peroxide, light and high pH varies with fluorophore but only minimally with the antibody to which the fluorophore is coupled.
source: The efficiency of fluorophore inactivation by hydrogen peroxide, light and high pH varies with fluorophore but only minimally with the antibody to which the fluorophore is coupled (Alexa Fluor 488 is inactivated more slowly than Alexa Fluor 570 or 647; Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations on fluorophore inactivation efficiency.

claim: Incubation of specimens in bleaching conditions for 60 min is sufficient to reduce fluorescence intensity by 10² to 10³-fold.
source: We typically incubate specimens in bleaching conditions for 60 min, which is sufficient to reduce fluorescence intensity by 102 to 103-fold (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the quantitative effect of bleaching duration on fluorescence intensity.

claim: The primary limitation on the number of t-CyCIF cycles that can be performed is the integrity of the tissue.
source: The primary limitation on the number of t-CyCIF cycles that can be performed is the integrity of the tissue: some tissues samples are physically more robust and can withstand more staining and washing procedures than others (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript identifies tissue integrity as the main limiting factor for cycle number.

claim: Normal tonsil, skin, glioblastoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer and melanoma can be subjected to >15 cycles with less than 25% cell loss.
source: As a rule, we find that normal tonsil, skin, glioblastoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer and melanoma can be subjected to >15 cycles with less than 25% cell loss.
evidence: The manuscript reports empirical findings on tissue robustness across different tissue types.

claim: A melanoma specimen can be subjected to 20 t-CyCIF cycles with good preservation of cell and tissue morphology.
source: Figure 4F shows a melanoma specimen subjected to 20 t-CyCIF cycles with good preservation of cell and tissue morphology (Figure 4G).
evidence: The manuscript presents a specific example of a melanoma specimen undergoing 20 cycles.

claim: The repeatability of staining a single specimen using the same set of antibodies shows high correlation (ρ = 0.95 to 0.99 for PCNA).
source: For PCNA, the correlation in staining intensities across four cycles was high (ρ = 0.95 to 0.99) and somewhat lower in the case of Vimentin and Tubulin (ρ = 0.80 to 0.95; Figure 6A; a more extensive comparison is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative correlation coefficients for repeated staining.

claim: For some antibodies, staining intensity increases rather than decreases with cycle number.
source: Thus, for at least a subset of antibodies, staining intensity increases rather than decreases with cycle number whereas background fluorescence falls.
evidence: The manuscript reports an unexpected observation about staining intensity changes.

claim: Dynamic range frequently increases with cycle number in t-CyCIF.
source: As a consequence, dynamic range, defined here as the ratio of the least to the most intense 5% of pixels, frequently increases with cycle number (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports an observed trend in dynamic range across cycles.

claim: The overlap in intensity distributions between slides A and B for the same antibodies and cycle number was high (>0.85).
source: When we compared staining between slides A and B for the same antibodies and cycle number, the overlap in intensity distributions was high (>0.85), demonstrating good sample to sample reproducibility (Zhou and Liu, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative overlap measurements demonstrating reproducibility.

claim: For eight antibodies, the overlap in intensity distributions was <0.6 when used in different cycles.
source: In the case of eight antibodies for which the effect of cycle number was greatest (including tubulin, as discussed above), the overlap in intensity distributions was <0.6 as a consequence of both increases and decreases in staining intensity (Figure 6E).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements of antibody performance variability.

claim: E-cadherin, keratin and β-catenin levels are highly correlated with each other in the PDAC specimen.
source: The analysis in Figure 7E shows that E-cadherin, keratin and β-catenin levels are highly correlated with each other, whereas vimentin and VEGFR2 receptor levels are anti-correlated, recapitulating the known dichotomy between epithelial and mesenchymal cell states in normal and diseased tissues.
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results from the PDAC specimen.

claim: Vimentin and VEGFR2 receptor levels are anti-correlated in the PDAC specimen.
source: The analysis in Figure 7E shows that E-cadherin, keratin and β-catenin levels are highly correlated with each other, whereas vimentin and VEGFR2 receptor levels are anti-correlated, recapitulating the known dichotomy between epithelial and mesenchymal cell states in normal and diseased tissues.
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results from the PDAC specimen.

claim: The levels of pERKT202/Y204 and pS6S235/S236 show high correlation (r = 0.81) in the PDAC specimen.
source: Many other physiologically relevant correlations are also observed, for example between the levels of pERKT202/Y204 (the phosphorylated, active form of the kinase) and activating phosphorylation of the downstream kinase pS6S235/S236 (r = 0.81).
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific correlation coefficient between two signaling proteins.

claim: CD45+ immune cells are more heavily infiltrated in the microenvironment of PDAC than in normal pancreas.
source: The microenvironment of PDAC was more heavily infiltrated with CD45+ immune cells than the normal pancreas, and the intestinal mucosa of the small intestine was also replete with immune cells, consistent with the known architecture and organization of this tissue.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from t-CyCIF imaging of PDAC and normal pancreas.

claim: In the α-SMAlow domain of renal cell carcinoma, CD3+ or CD8+ lymphocytes were fourfold enriched compared to the α-SMAhigh domain.
source: In the α-SMAlow domain, CD3+ or CD8+ lymphocytes were fourfold enriched (Figure 9C) and PD-1 and PD-L1-positive cells were 13 to 20-fold more prevalent as compared to the surrounding tumor stroma (α-SMAhigh domain)
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative enrichment measurements in different tumor regions.

claim: PD-1 and PD-L1-positive cells were 13 to 20-fold more prevalent in the α-SMAlow domain compared to the α-SMAhigh domain in renal cell carcinoma.
source: In the α-SMAlow domain, CD3+ or CD8+ lymphocytes were fourfold enriched (Figure 9C) and PD-1 and PD-L1-positive cells were 13 to 20-fold more prevalent as compared to the surrounding tumor stroma (α-SMAhigh domain)
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative enrichment measurements in different tumor regions.

claim: Co-localization of PD-1/PD-L1 was ~2.7-fold more likely in tumor than stroma in renal cell carcinoma.
source: We found that co-localization of PD-1/PD-L1 was ~2.7-fold more likely (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) in tumor and stroma and was concentrated on the tumor-stroma border consistent with previous reports on melanoma (Tumeh et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative co-localization analysis results.

claim: High-grade pancreatic and stomach cancers were intermingled in t-SNE space and could not be readily distinguished.
source: For example, while healthy and low-grade pancreatic and stomach cancer occupied distinct t-SNE domains, high-grade pancreatic and stomach cancers were intermingled and could not be readily distinguished (Figure 10F), recapitulating the known difficulty in distinguishing high-grade gastrointestinal tumors of diverse origin by histophathology (Varadhachary and Raber, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript reports t-SNE clustering results and relates them to known histopathological challenges.

claim: Semi-supervised clustering using EMGM modeling of all cells in the GBM tumor yielded eight distinct clusters, four of which encompassed 85% of all cells.
source: Semi-supervised clustering using expectation–maximization Gaussian mixture (EMGM) modeling of all cells in the tumor yielded eight distinct clusters, four of which encompassed 85% of all cells (Figure 12A and Figure 12—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of clustering analysis on GBM tumor cells.

claim: The presence of four highly populated t-CyCIF clusters in GBM is consistent with data from single-cell RNA-sequencing of ~400 cells from five GBMs.
source: The presence of four highly populated t-CyCIF clusters is consistent with data from single-cell RNA-sequencing of ~400 cells from five GBMs (Patel et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript compares their clustering results to published single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: Extensive intermixing of GBM cell clusters was observed at all spatial scales.
source: To study the relationship between phenotypic diversity and tumor architecture, we mapped each cell to an EMGM cluster (denoted by color). Extensive intermixing was observed at all spatial scales (Figure 12B).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from spatial mapping of cell clusters.

claim: Field of view 147 in the GBM specimen revealed extensive intermixing of four cluster types on a scale of ~3–5 cell diameters.
source: For example, field of view 147 was highly enriched for cells corresponding to cluster 5 (yellow), but a higher magnification view revealed extensive intermixing of four other cluster types on a scale of ~3–5 cell diameters (Figure 12C).
evidence: The manuscript reports detailed spatial analysis of a specific field of view.

claim: The fraction of cells from each cluster varied dramatically across macroscopic tumor regions in GBM.
source: At the level of larger, macroscopic tumor regions, the fraction of cells from each cluster also varied dramatically (Figure 12D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative variation in cluster composition across tumor regions.

claim: GBM is phenotypically heterogeneous on a spatial scale of 5–1000 cell diameters.
source: These results have several implications. First, they suggest that GBM is phenotypically heterogeneous on a spatial scale of 5–1000 cell diameters and that cells corresponding to distinct t-CyCIF clusters are often found in the vicinity of each other.
evidence: The manuscript draws conclusions from their spatial analysis of GBM heterogeneity.

claim: Over 200 commercial antibodies have been shown to be compatible with t-CyCIF.
source: To date, we have shown that over 200 commercial antibodies are compatible with the method as judged by patterns of staining similar to those previously reported for IHC
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of antibodies tested and validated for t-CyCIF.

claim: t-CyCIF can be performed using existing fluorescence microscopes.
source: First, t-CyCIF can be performed using existing fluorescence microscopes. Not only does this reduce costs and barriers to entry, it allows the unique strengths of slide-scanning, confocal, and structured illumination microscopes to be exploited.
evidence: The discussion section highlights the advantage of using existing microscopes.

claim: Approximately 90% of sporadic PDACs harbor driver mutations in KRAS.
source: Approximately 90% of sporadic PDACs also harbor driver mutations in KRAS, activating the MAPK pathway and promoting tumourigenesis (Vogelstein et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on KRAS mutations in PDAC.

claim: Expression of PD-L1 correlates with responsiveness to the immune checkpoint inhibitors pembrolizumab and nivolumab.
source: For example, expression of PD-L1 correlates with responsiveness to the ICIs pembrolizumab and nivolumab (Mahoney and Atkins, 2014) but the negative predictive value of PD-L1 expression alone is insufficient to stratify patient populations (Sharma and Allison, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on PD-L1 as a biomarker.

claim: The negative predictive value of PD-L1 expression alone is insufficient to stratify patient populations for immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy.
source: For example, expression of PD-L1 correlates with responsiveness to the ICIs pembrolizumab and nivolumab (Mahoney and Atkins, 2014) but the negative predictive value of PD-L1 expression alone is insufficient to stratify patient populations (Sharma and Allison, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on limitations of PD-L1 as a biomarker.

claim: The WNT pathway is frequently activated in PDAC.
source: The WNT pathway is frequently activated in PDAC and is important for oncogenic transformation of gastrointestinal tumours (Jones et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on WNT pathway activation in PDAC.

claim: Components of the tumor microenvironment strongly influence the initiation, progression and metastasis of cancer.
source: Multiple studies have established that these components of the tumor microenvironment strongly influence the initiation, progression and metastasis of cancer (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011) and the magnitude of responsiveness or resistance to immunotherapies (Tumeh et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on the role of the tumor microenvironment.

claim: Single-cell transcriptome profiling usually requires disaggregation of tissues, resulting in loss of spatial context.
source: However, single-cell sequencing usually requires disaggregation of tissues, resulting in loss of spatial context (Tirosh et al., 2016; Patel et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature on limitations of single-cell sequencing.
